name: Port Halden Taxi Fleet Stabilization Ordinance
enacted: five months before the effective date

source_sentences: The number of taxi licenses is fixed at the number outstanding on the effective date, and applies to anyone offering taxi service: street hails and taxi ranks.
New licenses are issued only by council vote.
Licenses become "medallions" that may be sold or leased, with transfers registered and a 2% transfer fee.
Vehicles that take only bookings made at least 30 minutes ahead, at a fare agreed at booking, may operate with an uncapped private-hire permit ($300 a year).
The Taxi and Limousine Office enforces the ordinance with 12 inspectors.
Enforcement is funded from the general budget and license fees.
The ordinance was introduced by the council five months before it took effect, with passage widely expected.
Fares are set by the city council as a meter rate, indexed each year to consumer prices; this rule predates the ordinance and is unchanged by it.

unclear.text: Whether a booking made through a smartphone app a few minutes before pickup meets the 30-minute rule.
readings: U1-a: app booking counts as pre-booked.

context: Port Halden is a city of about 900,000 people.
Until now, anyone who passed a driver background check and a vehicle inspection could obtain a city taxi license for $400 a year; about 2,400 licenses are in use.
Demand for taxi trips has grown about 3% a year with population and tourism.
Fares are set by the city council as a meter rate, indexed each year to consumer prices; this rule predates the ordinance and is unchanged by it.
The suburbs of Brindlewick and Corvale license their own taxis, which may drop passengers in Port Halden but may not pick up there.
